headline: Samsung banning smart TV apps that expose users' internet connections
summary: A vulnerability allowed apps to route outside traffic through users' home internet, turning TVs into proxy nodes. Samsung is now banning such apps.
details: Samsung is enhancing the security of its smart TV app platform following the discovery of a vulnerability that could expose users' internet connections. A cybersecurity firm, Mnemonic, found that certain apps could route strangers' web traffic through a user's home internet, making those requests appear to originate from the user.

The vulnerability was particularly concerning as it was found in apps featured in Samsung's app store, including a Pac-Man game. Installing such apps could, with a simple switch, turn a smart TV into a residential proxy exit node, potentially compromising user privacy and security.

In response to the findings, Samsung has stated it will ban any apps that share its users' internet connections. The company also announced plans to implement strict platform-wide developer policies that explicitly prohibit the use of residential proxy SDKs.

This issue is not unique to Samsung; LG recently announced similar measures to suspend apps that turn customer TVs into residential proxies. The use of residential proxies, especially through free VPNs, has become a growing concern in the cybersecurity landscape.

The vulnerability was particularly concerning as it was found in apps featured in Samsung's app store, including a Pac-Man game. Installing such apps could, with a simple switch, turn a smart TV into a residential proxy exit node, potentially compromising user privacy and security.

In response to the findings, Samsung has stated it will ban any apps that share its users' internet connections. The company also announced plans to implement strict platform-wide developer policies that explicitly prohibit the use of residential proxy SDKs.

This issue is not unique to Samsung; LG recently announced similar measures to suspend apps that turn customer TVs into residential proxies. The use of residential proxies, especially through free VPNs, has become a growing concern in the cybersecurity landscape.
